items.title: Fishermen Miraculously Spot Cruise Ship Pianist Who Spent 9 Hours in Open Sea After Falling Overboard
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: "I thought I was gonna die."
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Sean Norton and Grant Garrett were fishing for marlin near Catalina Island off the coast of Los Angeles when they spotted something floating in the water. That something, though, turned out to be a someone.

The men, returning from a morning fishing trip, spotted the man on Nov. 6. The man treading water in the Pacific Ocean identified himself as a Royal Caribbean employee, a pianist, who had fallen overboard from the ship he was working on, CBS LA reported.

They found — and rescued — the man about 20 miles off the coast in the middle of the ocean.

“I’m like, ‘Yeah, it’s a human being. Stop the boat; let’s get all of our lines in,'” Garrett recalled. Norton said, “Grant and I each got an arm and lifted him up,” adding, “The only thing he said to me was, ‘Thank you. I thought I was gonna die.”

Garrett and Norton called for emergency assistance and Newport Beach lifeguards responded to help them. Battalion Chief Adam Yacenda told the local CBS News affiliate they believe the Ovation of the Seas musician likely fell off the ship about nine hours earlier, at around 2:30 a.m.

The man, whose name hasn’t been disclosed, was transported to the Orange County Global Medical Center for care and is expected to make a miraculous recovery, according to the U.S. Coast Guard.

“You have this crazy super El Niño year,” said Norton. “This guy was in the water for probably 10 hours, but the water’s 76 degrees. A different year, no way he makes it.”

A spokesperson for Royal Caribbean said, “We are providing support and assistance to our crew member during this difficult time. To respect the privacy of our employee, we have no additional details to share.”

When Norton and Garrett pulled the man out, Norton remembered he was clearly in shock and said the only words he spoke were, “Thank you; I thought I was gonna die.”

items.title: Ezekiel 37 Prophecy About Israel’s Return Sparks Colton Dixon’s Latest Hit
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Interesting.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Singer Colton Dixon’s new song “Bones” comes at a time when the world feels, in many ways, like it’s on fire. The catchy tune is inspired by the valley of dry bones prophecy in Ezekiel 37.

Many Bible experts believe this chapter references Israel’s return to the land in 1948, and Dixon — who agrees — told CBN News some of his other reasons for connecting these Scriptures to “Bones.”

“It was kind of like the… the push to get off the sidelines as a believer, and to start prophesying over the dead things in my life,” he said of the song’s inspiration. “It comes from Ezekiel 37. … God gives Ezekiel a vision, brings him out into the middle of a desert full of a valley of dry bones, and tells him to start prophesying.”

Dixon continued, “So, as Ezekiel starts to prophesy, the bones start to rattle, they come together, and a whole army stands up around him.”

The singer believes the moment was prophetic for Israel “coming back and regaining their stance.” But he said the meaning can also run deeper, noting that Ezekiel’s hard-hitting message inspired him.

“As a believer, I’m like, ‘Man, I feel like we have this authority, spiritually, to prophesy over the dead things in our life,'” he said. “Galatians talks … about God getting us the keys to the kingdom. Whatever we bind on earth shall be bound in heaven. Whatever we loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven. So I’m like, ‘All right, it’s time to stop sitting on the sidelines as a believer.'”

Dixon said it’s easy for Christians to fall into what he described as an “autopilot lifestyle” — something he wants to help people navigate.

“That’s not the way God designed it,” he said, comparing it to a car’s autopilot feature. “It’s a great feature for your car, I might add, but that’s not the way God designed us to … live our lives. You’re just going to miss out on God’s best for you doing it that way.”

He’s hoping “Bones” gets people thinking more about the importance of living out biblical truth.

“God has something incredible for you,” Dixon said. “And I don’t want to settle for…bad or good when I can have God’s best.”

items.title: Indie Moses Sitcom ‘The Promised Land’ Is Moving to Prime Video — We Talk to the Show’s 33-Year-Old Creator
items.author: Cameron Strang
items.summary: Creator Mitch Hudson, an assistant director on The Chosen, made the show on the side for four years, with crew he recruited from the set and props borrowed from it.
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

For the last four years, Mitch Hudson has had two jobs. One was assistant director on The Chosen, the Bible series he joined in its first season in 2018. The other was a Moses workplace comedy he was making on the side, with money from friends and crew he recruited between setups.

That comedy, The Promised Land, moves to Prime Video in the U.S. on Nov. 15, the same day as The Chosen season six, distributed by Lionsgate. Season one, which Hudson created, wrote and directed, built its audience on YouTube, where every episode has passed 1 million views and the series has logged more than 150 million impressions.

Wasim No’Mani, who also appears in The Chosen, plays Moses in an Office-style mockumentary about leading a few million people out of Egypt and into a very long camping trip.

The show exists because of a change in Hudson himself, and he is specific about when it happened. It was during filming of The Chosen‘s second season. In the early years of The Chosen, Hudson kept his faith and his art in separate rooms.

“I grew up Christian, but I’m not gonna be a Christian writer or director. That’s just not my thing,” he said. “And then during season two of the show, while we were filming it, I had a big life event, epiphany, come to Jesus, whatever you want to call it. And I was like, if I want to make art, I should probably involve the Lord and make that a part of who I am and what I do.”

A friend had an idea for a Moses show. Hudson wrote the pilot. When his producers, who are also friends, found they had a little money (not much, he says), Hudson started recruiting from the one place he had access to: the crew of a hit Bible series.

“I was sneaking away, finding crew members in the shadowy corridors of set, just like, ‘Hey, do you wanna help me out with this pilot? I can’t pay you very much, but we can try to make it.’ I was so grateful, because I had been working as a crew member and gotten to know so many people on The Chosen who were then able to come and help me. And I kind of just gave all of it over and was like, all right, if this show happens, it’s God’s. Not to over-spiritualize that, people do that sometimes, but genuinely, I have tried on my own to make stuff. If I’m gonna make this, it’s gonna be with the Lord or it’s not gonna be made, probably.”

The Chosen helped in other ways. The pilot, shot in the fall of 2022 right after The Chosen wrapped its third season, ran on rented wardrobe and props from the series’ own stock.

“The producers were so kind to me because I had been working with them. They were like, ‘As long as it comes back undamaged and you get insurance in case it does get damaged, you can use our tents and you can use our props.’ And so we did. It’s actually funny, I have Moses’s prop staff right here. The Chosen owned it until the end of season seven, and then they gave a few of us who’d been on for the long run of the show one prop from the show that we could take home. I said, ‘I know exactly what I want.'”

Another piece of advice came from Dallas Jenkins, The Chosen‘s creator, on set during that same stretch.

“He said, ‘I love what you’re doing, and I think it’s a really great idea.’ And he gave me advice I’ve tried to hold on to ever since. He said, you need to meet the faith audience where they are and then push them. You can’t come out of the gate like, ‘I’m gonna do something that’s never been done in faith.’ It can’t just be radical. You’re either with it or you’re not. You have to meet the audience where they are and encourage them into a new direction. And that new direction for The Promised Land is into humor, which is always scary for faith, because usually the joke is on faith. It’s not usually with faith. That’s what makes our show a little bit different.”

Hudson has a test for where the line falls, and he applies it to every joke.

“My line is usually just: what is the joke about? Is it a joke that would make less of God or the things that are in the Bible? Or is it a joke that is poking at what people are like? I essentially put every single joke in the show into that second category. The joke is never on the Lord. The joke is never on the idea of faith. The joke is never, ‘How could someone believe this? This is crazy.’ The joke is all about what people are like in these situations.”

The platform change to Prime Video comes with a trade-off. Season one is leaving YouTube.

“I’ve loved that we’ve been freely available, but having season one focused on Prime helps us get a little more placement as a TV show, especially in people’s minds when they see it on a streamer. And that is a big part of helping us get season two out.”

Season two, shot in Morocco, is nearly done but has no release date. Hudson has a hope for the weeks ahead: on Prime, the show will sit next to a season of The Chosen he expects to hit hard.

“I worked on all of that. It is going to be such a great season of The Chosen, but it’s also going to be so emotional that I kind of hope people watch The Promised Land on Prime as a palette cleanser. Watch every episode of The Chosen as soon as it drops, and then in between, settle in with a little bit of The Promised Land. That’s the hope, at least.”

He has even floated a graphic for the show’s social pages of Moses holding out a tissue box.

His larger plan — five seasons and about 40 episodes of The Promised Land with a feature film in the middle — depends on viewers, Hudson says. The show is still independent, essentially him and a small team, with Lionsgate as distribution partner.

“We’re not a crowdfunded show, but we are a crowd-supported show, if that makes sense. When season one comes out on Prime, everyone goes to Prime and they watch the episodes. Even if they’ve seen them before, they rewatch them. Literally, if the people show up, we can keep making it.”

items.title: Tuesday, November 10, 2026
items.author: Bishop Robert Barron
items.summary:
Bishop Robert Barron

Friends, today’s Gospel describes the obedience of a faithful servant.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Bishop Robert Barron

Daily Reading


First Reading
TiTUS 2:1-8, 11-14

But as for you, teach what is consistent with sound doctrine. Tell the older men to be temperate, serious, prudent, and sound in faith, in love, and in endurance. Likewise, tell the older women to be reverent in behavior, not to be slanderers or slaves to drink; they are to teach what is good, so that they may encourage the young women to love their husbands, to love their children, to be self-controlled, chaste, good managers of the household, kind, being submissive to their husbands, so that the word of God may not be discredited.

Likewise, urge the younger men to be self-controlled. Show yourself in all respects a model of good works, and in your teaching show integrity, gravity, and sound speech that cannot be censured; then any opponent will be put to shame, having nothing evil to say of us.

For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to all, training us to renounce impiety and worldly passions, and in the present age to live lives that are self-controlled, upright, and godly, while we wait for the blessed hope and the manifestation of the glory of our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ. He it is who gave himself for us that he might redeem us from all iniquity and purify for himself a people of his own who are zealous for good deeds.

Psalm
PsALM 37:3-4, 18 and 23, 27 and 29

Trust in the Lord, and do good;
so you will live in the land, and enjoy security.
Take delight in the Lord,
and he will give you the desires of your heart.
The Lord knows the days of the blameless,
and their heritage will abide forever;
Our steps are made firm by the Lord,
when he delights in our way;
Depart from evil, and do good;
so you shall abide forever.
The righteous shall inherit the land,
and live in it forever.

Gospel Reading
LUkE 17:7-10

“Who among you would say to your slave who has just come in from plowing or tending sheep in the field, ‘Come here at once and take your place at the table’? Would you not rather say to him, ‘Prepare supper for me, put on your apron and serve me while I eat and drink; later you may eat and drink’? Do you thank the slave for doing what was commanded? So you also, when you have done all that you were ordered to do, say, ‘We are worthless slaves; we have done only what we ought to have done!’ ”

Reflection

Friends, today’s Gospel describes the obedience of a faithful servant. Our lives are not about us; they are about the King. We are built not for commanding others but for obedience. In the presence of the awesome lordliness of God—that mind and will whose grandeur we can barely fathom—we bow, we listen, we surrender.

The Lord is the King, the one who commands, directs, and oversees, and who, accordingly, demands obedience. For a military tribe such as the ancient Hebrews, this term had, to be sure, an especially powerful resonance. The proper response to a king is obedience. The king commands, and the servant responds—simply, promptly, unhesitatingly.

A courtier or a messenger might not understand the rationale for or consequences of what the king has told him to do, but he does it, trusting in the wisdom and power of the one who sends him. The word “obey” is derived from the Latin obedire, to listen attentively, to heed. In the presence of God the Lord, we his servants should listen, bending our ears and our wills to his word.

items.title: A Liturgy of a Nation’s Soul: Jefferson, Ratzinger, and the Limits of Institutionalism
items.author: Peter Grajzl
items.summary:
Peter Grajzl

An interpretation of Ratzinger’s theology on life, liberty, and happiness offers a compelling illumination of the American promise.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Peter Grajzl

In 1776, a group of revolutionaries in Philadelphia declared a truth they held self-evident: Human beings are equal in their inherent worth and endowed by their Creator with certain inalienable rights, among which are “Life, Liberty, and the pursuit of Happiness.” Now, as the United States marks 250 years of an unprecedented political experiment, those ideas warrant renewed reflection. 

Over the ensuing two and a half centuries, the American project has evolved into a global symbol of liberal democracy, constitutional order, and economic freedom. To secure the Jeffersonian promise, modern societies strive to shape the political, legal, and economic conditions that govern social life. We largely place our hope in what Nobel Prize-winning economist Douglass North defines as the humanly devised “rules of the game” (e.g., constitutions, laws, and regulations), expecting that the right institutional framework will protect our rights and foster prosperity.1

Yet underneath our complex institutional framework lies a persistent, quiet crisis of meaning.2 As shared prosperity proves elusive, political antagonism mounts, and social cohesion weakens, we must ask: Can purely institutional solutions ever deliver the fullness of life, liberty, and happiness we long for? Or have we mistaken institutional means for the deeper ends of human flourishing?

A profound answer may be inferred from the late Joseph Ratzinger’s (Pope Benedict XVI’s) “My Joy Is to Be in Thy Presence: On the Christian Belief in Eternal Life.” First published as a chapter in God Is Near Us: The Eucharist, the Heart of Life, this eloquent and penetrating essay draws from Ratzinger’s homiletic work from decades earlier.

Naturally, Ratzinger never addresses Jefferson directly. However, an interpretation of Ratzinger’s theology on life, liberty, and happiness offers a compelling illumination of the American promise. Viewing the Jeffersonian triad through Ratzinger’s theology suggests that many of the struggles and discontents of modern life are not merely institutional in origin, but also reflect a diminished sense of transcendence. Catholicism does not offer a replacement for sound institutions and government policies but a more expansive account of meaning that situates both within a broader vision of human flourishing.

Recovering Life:
From the Survival of Bios to the Gift of Zoē

When Jefferson wrote of the right to life, the immediate context was protection against the arbitrary exercise of power and the violence of tyranny. In the modern liberal tradition, this right entails the preservation of physical existence and bodily integrity—the finite realm of bios, which Ratzinger describes as “the passing life of this world” (140).

Ratzinger identifies a fundamental reductionism in the corresponding conceptualization of life. We have devoted much effort into preserving biological life, yet grow increasingly “uncertain” (130) of what lies beyond it. Even among Christians, he notes, “the awareness of eternal life has become astoundingly weak” (131). Citing Hans Urs von Balthasar, Ratzinger observes:

It is as if modern man had had a tendon cut, so that he can no longer run toward his original goal, as if his wings had been clipped, as if his spiritual awareness of transcendence had withered (130).

This fading hope in eternity, Ratzinger notes, is the reverse side of a weakened faith in the living God. When we cease to believe in God as “an active agent in history” (131), we shut ourselves into a world where only what we can build, touch, and measure is real.

Ratzinger thus points to the Gospel of John for a far richer concept: zoē, (“rooted in eternal life”). Rather than being a chronological extension of bios, eternal life entails “a new quality of existence . . . freed from the fragmentation of . . . the accelerating flight of moments” (137). Eternal life is the “true life” that forms “the firm base of our soul” and “an indestructible heart from which spring the courage and joy to go on, even when exterior things are painful and hard” (140, 137). 

We do not discover this life by looking inward at our private wants but by “learn[ing] to see God once more as an active agent in the world and in regard to ourselves” (132). As Ratzinger emphasizes, already amidst our fleeting temporal existence, eternal life is made present “whenever we truly encounter God from within” (140).

Reclaiming Liberty:
The Myth of Utopia vs. Liberation from Self

If Jefferson’s conception of life provides the foundation of the American experiment, liberty constitutes its central organizing principle. In the secular tradition, liberty is often defined negatively as the absence of coercion, or positively as self-determination.

Yet in human history, the pursuit of absolute liberty has not infrequently devolved into destructive, totalitarian ideologies. Why do our institutional efforts to build perfectly free societies often result in new forms of captivity?
Word on Fire’s Liturgy of the Hours is Here!
Order Your Set Today

Ratzinger answers by exposing the delusion of utopia. Modernity has attempted to replace eschatology with self-made political utopias, based on the belief that an “inner logic in history” (142) will inevitably produce a just society through the right institutional arrangements. But this, Ratzinger asserts, is a “primitive myth” and “simply illogical” (142): 

The struggle to keep evil under control, within limits, has to be taken up anew by each generation and can never be removed by the institutional arrangements of an earlier generation.

For Ratzinger, utopia resembles the myth of Tantalus. The perfect, self-made free society, intended to “fulfill man’s hope by its own powers and without faith in God” (142), always seems within reach, yet proves elusive, in part because “man always remains free and can therefore never be fixed in place in a final state of things” (142). Utopia has proven unreachable via institutional engineering.

True liberty, Ratzinger argues, is found not in the reconstruction of external social structures, but in internal transformation⎯liberation from the self:

Thus it becomes apparent that there is in this face-to-face encounter with God nothing selfish, no withdrawal into a merely private realm, but that very liberation from the self which alone makes any sense of eternity (141).

The contrast with the modern ideal of autonomous individualism is unmistakable. Under the banner of individual liberty, modern culture has instead built what Ratzinger calls a “dungeon of loneliness” (136), manifested, among other things, in the social fragmentation that the political scientist Robert Putnam captured in his phrase “bowling alone.” We demand the freedom to do what we want, but this self-centered liberty eventually isolates us, turning others into obstacles or competitors.

True liberation occurs, Ratzinger stresses, when our individual wills are aligned with the divine will of the living God. When we step into the “sanctuary” of prayer and place ourselves in the “pilgrim company of God’s history” (138), we are freed from purely private questioning. There, we no longer see others through the lens of “mine and yours”—what John Chrysostom called “cold words”—but as members of “one Body” (141). 

In Ratzinger’s theology, true liberty is the freedom to love, to sacrifice, and to unite our gaze “with the single gaze and the one being of the Son” (144). The genuinely “liberating force” thus arises within the “quiet cycle of true life,” in an economy of grace where “Nothing that is good goes for nothing” (145).

Refocusing the Pursuit of Happiness:
The Illusory vs. the Presence

For Jefferson and the broader political philosophy of the American founding, the pursuit of happiness encompassed the freedom to acquire property, cultivate virtue, and seek human flourishing. In contemporary society, however, the pursuit has largely been narrowed to a race for wealth, status, and material comfort.

Ratzinger meets this reality with startling clarity: “We long for justice; and that is why we also long for truth. . . . We long for true happiness,” he adds, “All of us” (135, 136). Yet we are constantly tempted to settle for cheap replacements:

The happiness of mere success, of mere power, of mere wealth, is always an illusory happiness; a glance at the world of today . . . will show us how true this is (139).

To illustrate true happiness, Ratzinger turns to Psalm 73. The righteous man’s temporal life has become a painful contradiction; he suffers illness and anguish while the cynics, who mock God, grow “healthy and plump” (138). On the verge of despair, the supplicant wonders if it was pointless to remain righteous. The decisive moment comes when he enters the sanctuary of God. Stepping beyond his private calculations, “the true perspective of reality re-emerges” (139).

Nevertheless I am continually with you; you hold my right hand. . . . Whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing upon earth that I desire besides you. My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion for ever. . . . For me it is good to be near God (139; Ps 73: 23-26, 28).

This, Ratzinger insists, is the exact definition of true happiness: “my happiness is to be in your presence” (139). 
Magnificent Humanity
Get Pope Leo’s Encyclical

Toward a Liturgy of a Nation’s Soul

The 250th anniversary of the United States provides an opportunity not only for celebration but also for reflection on what we truly seek. Every society has, in a sense, its own liturgy: a pattern of loves and commitments that reveals what it ultimately prioritizes. The modern secular imagination has directed much of its confidence in institutions—the “rules of the game” that organize our political, legal, and economic affairs. These rules are essential for the orderly functioning of a temporal society. Yet they cannot, by themselves, give us a reason to hope. 

Joseph Ratzinger’s theology provides a powerful complement to the secular horizons of modern thought. He invites us to recognize that life is not merely the preservation of earthly existence but allowing God to teach the soul and orient it toward eternal life. Similarly, liberty is found not in the unconstrained autonomy, but in the liberation that comes from opening oneself to God’s will. And happiness lies not in the fragile fulfillment promised by wealth and power but in the lasting joy of communion with God.

In a passage in his essay, Ratzinger looks back at St. Augustine, who lived through the chaotic collapse of Rome. Yet St. Augustine did not succumb to despair because he could see a new city arise at the horizon, the City of God. He was so warmed by this promise that he wrote, “Brothers, when I speak of this city, even though the troubles here grow great, I can no longer contain myself” (144).

As we navigate the challenges and anxieties of our own historical moment, perhaps we might look anew at our nation’s heritage of life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness—not as self-contained political ends, but as invitations to a fuller, transcendent horizon. By looking beyond the immediate calculus that characterizes our temporal concerns, we may open ourselves to the grace that Ratzinger’s theology and the Catholic tradition identify as essential for forming persons and communities capable of building a truly free and enduring society.

1  See, e.g., Daron Acemoglu and James A. Robinson, Why Nations Fail: The Origins of Power, Prosperity, and Poverty (New York: Crown Business, 2012); Daron Acemoglu and James A. Robinson, The Narrow Corridor: States, Societies, and the Fate of Liberty (New York: Penguin Press, 2019). Acemoglu and Robinson, together with Simon Johnson, likewise won a Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences “for studies of how institutions are formed and affect prosperity.”
2  See, e.g., Charles Taylor, A Secular Age (Cambridge, MA: Belknap Press of Harvard University Press, 2007); Alasdair MacIntyre, After Virtue: A Study in Moral Theory, 3rd ed. (Notre Dame, IN: University of Notre Dame Press, 2007).
